title: Web Security: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Attack Lab
description: A hands-on cyber range training lab based on the SEED Labs CSRF exercise with Elgg. Students perform GET and POST CSRF attacks, test secret tokens, and analyze SameSite cookies.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of HTTP requests (GET and POST)
Familiarity with HTML forms and JavaScript
Understanding of web browser developer tools
outcomes: Understand the fundamental mechanics of Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).
Forge an HTTP GET request to perform unauthorized state-changing actions.
Forge an HTTP POST request using JavaScript and hidden HTML forms.
Understand and re-enable server-side CSRF secret token verification.
Analyze SameSite cookie attributes (Strict vs Lax vs Normal) and their role in CSRF defense.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
# CSRF Attack Lab - Introduction

## Disclaimer
This lab is for **educational purposes only** in an isolated cyber range sandbox.

## Storyline
You are a security researcher assessing the **Elgg** social network platform. The application is vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).

You will act as an attacker (**Samy**) targeting a victim (**Alice**) who has an active session on Elgg.

## Lab Topology & Environment
- **seed** (10.1.30.10): Your workstation running Ubuntu with Firefox and tools.
- **server** (10.1.30.5): Web server hosting Elgg and the attacker site.

### Accessible Sites:
- `http://www.seed-server.com` - Vulnerable Elgg application
- `http://www.attacker32.com` - Attacker malicious website
- `http://www.example32.com` - Defense demonstration site

### Pre-configured Accounts:
- Alice: `alice` / `seedalice`
- Samy: `samy` / `seedsamy`
- Admin: `admin` / `seedelgg`
- Boby: `boby` / `seedboby`

levels.title: Access the Sandbox
levels.cloud_content:
## Connecting to Your Sandbox

1. In the topology view, right-click **seed** and choose **Open GUI**.
2. Login credentials: username **user**, password **Password123**.
3. Open Firefox and verify that `http://www.seed-server.com` loads.
4. When ready, submit **start** to begin the training.

levels.title: Task 1: Observing HTTP Requests
levels.content:
# Task 1: Observing HTTP Requests

Before forging requests, investigate legitimate Elgg requests using Firefox Developer Tools (press F12 -> Network tab).

1. Log in to `http://www.seed-server.com` as **alice** / **seedalice**.
2. In Developer Tools Network tab, watch the request when Alice adds a friend or clicks Add Friend.
3. Note the HTTP method, URL endpoint, and parameters.

Submit the HTTP method used by the Add-Friend action (in UPPERCASE) as the flag.
levels.solution: The Add-Friend request uses the HTTP GET method: http://www.seed-server.com/action/friends/add?friend=...

hints.title: HTTP Method Hint
hints.content: Check the Method column in Firefox Network Developer Tools. Is it GET or POST?

levels.title: Task 2: CSRF Attack via GET Request
levels.content: # Task 2: CSRF Attack via GET Request Samy wants Alice to add him as a friend without her consent. 1. Find Samy's GUID on Elgg (visit Samy's profile — it appears in the URL). 2. Edit `/home/user/Labsetup/attacker/addfriend.html` on the seed machine. 3. Set the `` tag `src` to: `http://www.seed-server.com/action/friends/add?friend=&__elgg_ts=&__elgg_token=` (get a valid token+ts by clicking Add Friend while logged in as Alice and reading them from DevTools). 4. Log in as Alice in Firefox, then visit `http://www.attacker32.com/addfriend.html` in a new tab. 5. Alice's browser silently sends the GET request and adds Samy as a friend. 6. Confirm the attack worked: log in as Samy and check Friends list — Alice should appear. 7. Get your flag: ```bash curl http://localhost:8888/flag/2 ``` The daemon verifies the friend relationship exists in the database before releasing the flag.
levels.solution: Embed into addfriend.html. When Alice visits http://www.attacker32.com/addfriend.html, her browser sends the GET request with her session cookie.

hints.title: How to trigger GET automatically?
hints.content: An HTML `` tag automatically sends a GET request to its `src` on page load — no user interaction needed.

hints.title: Finding Samy GUID
hints.content: Log in as Samy, go to Samy's profile page. The GUID is the number in the URL: `/profile/samy` → check the Add Friend URL to find the numeric id.

hints.title: Retrieving the flag
hints.content: Once the attack worked (Alice added Samy), run on the seed terminal: `curl http://localhost:8888/flag/2`

levels.title: Task 3: CSRF Attack via POST Request
levels.content:
# Task 3: CSRF Attack via POST Request

Samy wants Alice's profile bio to be overwritten.

Profile edits use an HTTP POST to `http://www.seed-server.com/action/profile/edit`.

1. Inspect the profile-edit POST request in Firefox DevTools (submit a real edit as Alice first).
2. Complete `/home/user/Labsetup/attacker/editprofile.html`:
   - Set `guid` to Alice's GUID (find it in the profile edit URL).
   - The `briefdescription` field is **already set** to the flag string — do not change it.
3. While logged in as Alice, visit `http://www.attacker32.com/editprofile.html`.
4. The form auto-submits and overwrites Alice's bio.
5. **Go to Alice's Elgg profile** — the flag is now visible in her bio.

> The flag appears directly in Alice's profile page. You do not need to curl anything.

You can also confirm via the daemon:
```bash
curl http://localhost:8888/flag/3
```
levels.solution: Create a hidden form in JavaScript with fields name, briefdescription='Samy is my Hero', accesslevel[briefdescription]=2, and guid=ALICE_GUID, set form.action to http://www.seed-server.com/action/profile/edit, method='post', and call form.submit() on window.onload.

hints.title: Auto-submitting POST form
hints.content: Use `document.createElement('form')`, append hidden inputs, and call `form.submit()` inside `window.onload`.

hints.title: Required Fields
hints.content: Required fields: `name`, `briefdescription`, `accesslevel[briefdescription]=2`, and `guid` (Alice's numeric GUID from her profile URL).

hints.title: Retrieving the flag
hints.content: After the attack, go to Alice's Elgg profile — her bio will display the flag. Or run: `curl http://localhost:8888/flag/3`

levels.title: Task 4: Enable the CSRF Countermeasure
levels.content:
# Task 4: Enable the CSRF Countermeasure

Elgg has a built-in secret token defense (`__elgg_token` and `__elgg_ts`). It was intentionally disabled in `Csrf.php`.

1. Enter the Elgg container:
```bash
docker exec -it elgg-10.9.0.5 /bin/bash
```
2. Open the file:
```
/var/www/elgg/vendor/elgg/elgg/engine/classes/Elgg/Security/Csrf.php
```
3. Remove the bypass line at the top of `validate()`:
```php
return; // Added for SEED Labs (disabling the CSRF countermeasure)
```
4. Exit the container. The change takes effect immediately (no rebuild needed).
5. Re-run your Task 2 attack (visit `addfriend.html` as Alice again).
6. **The attack is now blocked** — Elgg shows an error page containing your Task 4 flag.

> The flag appears on the Elgg blocked-request page automatically when the defense is active.

You can also confirm via the daemon:
```bash
curl http://localhost:8888/flag/4
```
levels.solution: Remove the early return statement in validate() inside Csrf.php to re-enable token checking. Forged requests from attacker32.com lack valid tokens and are rejected.

hints.title: Container modification
hints.content: Run `docker exec -it elgg-10.9.0.5 /bin/bash` then use `nano` or `vi` to edit Csrf.php.

hints.title: Why does the attack fail?
hints.content: The Same-Origin Policy prevents `attacker32.com` from reading Alice's `__elgg_token` from `seed-server.com` pages — that's why the token defense works.

hints.title: Retrieving the flag
hints.content: After removing the bypass line, re-run the attack from Task 2. The error page Elgg shows will contain your flag. Or: `curl http://localhost:8888/flag/4`

levels.title: Task 5: SameSite Cookie Defense
levels.content:
# Task 5: SameSite Cookie Defense

Modern browsers enforce SameSite cookie attributes to mitigate CSRF.

**Step 1 — Set the cookies:**
Visit `http://www.seed-server.com/defense/` in Firefox. Three cookies are set: `cookie-normal`, `cookie-lax`, `cookie-strict`.

**Step 2 — Test from attacker32.com:**
On the page, click Link B → `http://www.attacker32.com/testing.html`.

**Step 3 — Submit a cross-site POST:**
On `testing.html`, click **Submit (POST)**. This sends a cross-site POST to `showcookies.php` on the server.

**Step 4 — Read the flag:**
The `showcookies.php` page detects that:
- The request came from `attacker32.com`
- `cookie-lax` and `cookie-strict` are **missing** (blocked by browser)

When both conditions are true, **the flag is printed directly on the page**.

> You do not need to curl anything. The flag appears in your browser.
levels.solution: Visiting example32.com sets 3 cookies. In cross-site requests from attacker32.com, SameSite=Strict and SameSite=Lax cookies are not attached to cross-site sub-requests, preventing CSRF.

hints.title: SameSite Cookie types
hints.content: `SameSite=Strict` blocks cookies on all cross-site requests. `SameSite=Lax` allows them on top-level GET navigation but blocks them on cross-site POST forms.

hints.title: Retrieving the flag
hints.content: Make sure you use the **POST** submit button on `testing.html` (option C), not the GET link. Only a cross-site POST blocks both `cookie-lax` and `cookie-strict`.
